challenges.argument_and_conditions:
A01 — amend the operational ceiling, retain the explicit preference

A01 and B01 share the useful new evidence: Cole explicitly objects to more than three items and repeated lists. A01's “three as a ceiling” is faithful if strictly limited to ordinary illustrative series. My concern is not its truth but the optimization it invites: generate three, distribute the rest, pronounce success. A01 already warns against that, so our disagreement is small. Do not dilute Cole's explicit preference into merely checking whether a long inventory feels useful.

**Negotiated replacement**, both Cole style references, existing example bullet:

> **Let examples develop the argument.** For Cole's prose, keep ordinary illustrative series to at most three items and avoid repeated lists within a paragraph; a shorter list can still be filler. Select the example that advances the point or explain the relationship the inventory stood in for. Do not merely spread the same inventory across sentences. Preserve required coverage and materially distinct reasons, developing or reorganizing them rather than silently dropping them. This is Cole's preference, not a rule for every author's voice.

This accepts the numerical operationalization that I initially left as a reported preference. It is a maximum, not an invitation to produce triads. R03's criticism identifies a sentence/pattern but does not prove he disliked exactly its enumeration. Keep that interpretation provisional. Do not claim R06's retained five-item list was approved merely because its whole passage was preferred.

**Redundancy:** replace the existing bullet; do not repeat it in entrypoints or both general references. General coverage/selection rules already exist. **What would change my view:** if fresh examples show omission of distinct reasons or count gaming despite this wording, remove the numeric operational command while retaining the author's explicit feedback and improve the worked example.

challenges.wording: Compare what the actual versions make recoverable, what they delay and what they might lose. Read a passage with its surroundings: what makes the next claim matter, or prepares the next event or turn? Moving or dividing material can change endorsement, timing or rhetorical force without changing the underlying facts. An unresolved reflection can become an apparent thesis; coordination can become an asserted sequence. Preserve supported relationships while pursuing a stronger arrangement. Choose independently when the brief settles the tradeoff; expose consequential unresolved intent rather than silently deciding a new belief.
challenges.argument_and_conditions:
A02 — challenge the added paragraph; accept a smaller comparison prompt

A02 increases an already complete comparison paragraph to about twice its size. Its best addition is “what makes the next claim matter”; most of the rest repeats current instructions to read the relevant whole, compare actual versions, preserve timing and rhetorical force, allow a better original and select by the brief. “When the original progresses better ... repair the actual defects” risks making fidelity to original movement the winning criterion. A newly structured version may be stronger precisely because its movement changes. R11 supports the author's preference on that passage, not a general mechanism requiring more conservation.

My B03 deferred any change. I can move to a **small replacement now as a candidate**, without claiming it demonstrated benefit. Replace the existing paragraph beginning “Compare what the actual versions make recoverable” in both structure references with:

> Compare what the actual versions make recoverable, what they delay and what they might lose. Read a passage with its surroundings: what makes the next claim matter, or prepares the next event or turn? Moving or dividing material can change endorsement, timing or rhetorical force without changing the underlying facts. An unresolved reflection can become an apparent thesis; coordination can become an asserted sequence. Preserve supported relationships while pursuing a stronger arrangement. Choose independently when the brief settles the tradeoff; expose consequential unresolved intent rather than silently deciding a new belief.

The following existing paragraph already protects deliberate delay, repetition, humor and sound. Keep it. Existing “an improvement request does not demand a rewrite” handles original retention; do not duplicate it here.

**Boundary:** R11 is not the document ending. S03 continues with the chatbot countercase and further argument. A's initial comparison mostly avoids the error, but any negotiated “ending preservation” rule would be unsupported. R11's long sentence may supply momentum; that remains our hypothesis. R09 shows splitting can work; R13 shows explanation need not become story.

**What would persuade me toward A's full wording:** fresh examples showing models recognize supported facts and local clarity but systematically fail to compare progression under the current instructions, and a demonstrated advantage of the fuller wording over this shorter replacement. Without that, instruction growth costs more than its evidence supports. I will accept the short candidate replacement as an operational clarification, not an empirical finding.

challenges.wording: An argument that “stayed with me from” a report was not necessarily “first encountered” there. Make the useful connection without adding unsupported personal history. A disclaimer is also a claim: follow an author's correction at its supported scope without inferring a credential or experience they have not specified, and retain independent qualifications that still apply. Repair the unsupported relationship while retaining useful changes around it.
challenges.argument_and_conditions:
A03 — amend, place beside source meaning, preserve the useful disclaimer distinction

A03 combines two issues. The unsupported personal-history examples concretize existing rules well. The disclaimer distinction is useful: an inherited disclaimer is itself a claim, not inherently privileged. My B02 omitted that distinction and would benefit from it. But the second half of A03 repeats request authority and clarification policy already in the entrypoints; adding it to development planning gives a narrow credential dispute undue prominence.

**Negotiated compact insertion**, writer `references/language-and-meaning.md` under “Evidence, inference and action” and editor `references/technical-meaning.md` after the actual-before/after paragraph:

> An argument that “stayed with me from” a report was not necessarily “first encountered” there. Make the useful connection without adding unsupported personal history. A disclaimer is also a claim: follow an author's correction at its supported scope without inferring a credential or experience they have not specified, and retain independent qualifications that still apply. Repair the unsupported relationship while retaining useful changes around it.

This supersedes my initial B02 example pair; I would remove the “former/both” example from the final compact insertion to avoid turning an unresolved referent into a simple answer key. Keep it in the evaluation evidence. The model audit interprets “former” as self-preferencing links and labels “both” defective. We can confidently identify the risk that “both” broadens the asserted relation beyond a singular referent; the source's awkward multi-item antecedent does not externally verify which attachment was intended. An ambiguity test should permit preserving or resolving the reference from context, not reward reciting the audit.

**Redundancy:** no new anti-invention rule, credential exception, global Cole fact or extra questioning gate. A03's “because of that” example is too generic here: ordinary supported causal development must remain easy, as R03 demonstrates. R06 is the positive control for using the full document to develop a stronger supported idea.

**What would change my view:** a source-conflict case where this compact wording fails to distinguish removing a disputed claim from inventing its opposite would justify A's fuller boundary text. It would not justify automatically asking about every disclaimer. R01's “yes I am” does not establish a particular credential; correcting the source brief is separate from judging the earlier generations.
